title: Third-Party AI Extensions
headings: Block AI extensions with your MDM
body: Third-Party AI Extensions AI browser extensions such as Grammarly, Sider, Monica and HARPA AI read the pages people open and the text they type, and send it to their own AI service. That path skips Whiteout. AI Footprint lists these extensions on every device so you can decide which to allow. They appear in Coverage → AI Footprint with the category Third-party AI extension . This never includes Whiteout's own extension. --- What's inventoried Desktop Guard 1.8.106 and later reads the installed extensions in every profile of every browser it scans (see Browser coverage for the list). It does this as part of its full scan, every 8 hours and when you choose Rescan . Only AI extensions are kept. An extension is reported only if: its ID matches an AI extension in Whiteout's catalog (shown as Known ), or its name looks like AI, for example it contains ChatGPT , Claude , Gemini , Copilot or Perplexity , or the word AI , GPT , LLM or Assistant (shown as unknown ). Every other extension is dropped on the device and never sent to Whiteout. Catalogued AI extensions include Claude for Chrome, ChatGPT, Grammarly, Sider, Monica, HARPA AI, Merlin, MaxAI, Liner, Compose AI, QuillBot, Wordtune, Jasper and Glasp. Extension IDs are added to the catalog only after they're confirmed in the Chrome Web Store, Microsoft Edge Add-ons or Firefox Add-ons. What each extension shows Open the extension's footprint row, or the finding, to see: Field Values --- --- Browser and Profile Which browser and which profile (by folder name, such as Default ) Profile account Work account , Personal account , Not signed in or Unknown account . Only this verdict leaves the device, never the email address. Install source Installed by policy (IT) , Web store , Sideloaded (installed by other software), Developer mode or Unknown Site access Can read every site or Limited to specific sites Version and Enabled The installed version, and whether it's turned on Extension ID The ID to use if you block it Can read every site An extension marked Can read every site has permission to read and change any page the person opens, including your internal apps, email and documents. It can send what it reads to its vendor. That's why such an extension raises a high severity finding. --- Findings A catalogued AI extension on a device raises Shadow AI — installed because no Whiteout surface checks what it sends. The exception is Claude for Chrome : Desktop Guard checks the prompts sent through it, so it counts as governed wherever Desktop Guard is live. Extension Severity --- --- Can read every site High A catalogued AI assistant rated Elevated risk (most of the list above) High A catalogued extension with standard risk, limited to specific sites Medium Unknown (AI-style name only) High, once another signal from the same device backs it up. A name alone stays in the inventory without a finding. See Unknown tools. What to do: 1. If it's sanctioned, allowlist it under Manage → Allowlisted tools . For a catalogued extension, use the catalog key shown in the finding's Tool column, for example grammarly extension. 2. If it isn't approved, remove it from the profile, and keep it out with your browser's extension policy (below). 3. If it's unknown and you know what it is, choose Add to catalog . --- Block AI extensions with your MDM Chrome and Edge read the same extension policies. Firefox has its own. Copy the Extension ID from the finding's evidence. Browser Policy How --- --- --- Chrome , Edge ExtensionInstallBlocklist A list of extension IDs people can't install. Chrome and Edge also turn off a blocklisted extension that's already installed. Chrome , Edge ExtensionSettings Per extension ID, set installation mode to blocked. Use this when you manage extensions with ExtensionSettings already. Firefox ExtensionSettings Per add-on ID, set installation mode to blocked. Policy locations are the same ones you use to force-install Whiteout. For example, Chrome uses the macOS domain com.google.Chrome and the Windows key HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Google\Chrome. See Force-install the extension. If you block all extensions (with in the blocklist) and allow only approved ones, add the Whiteout extension ID to ExtensionInstallAllowlist, or force-install it, so Whiteout keeps working. An extension can have a different ID in each store. A Chrome Web Store extension installed in Edge keeps its Chrome ID. Block the ID the finding shows. After you block an extension, its finding resolves at the next full scan that no longer finds it. Keep an extension off sensitive sites instead. If people may use an AI extension in general but it shouldn't run on your internal apps, the Browser AI policy setting can keep chosen extensions off the sites you list, through the MDM profiles Whiteout generates. See Keep AI extensions off sensitive sites. --- What isn't covered What the extension sends. Whiteout lists the extension and what it can access. It doesn't see what the extension reads or sends. Safari extensions, and browsers the profile scan doesn't read. See Browser coverage. AI panels built into the browser, such as the Copilot sidebar in Edge, Gemini in Chrome and Leo in Brave. These aren't extensions. AI Footprint lists them separately. See Built-in browser AI.

title: AI Inside Work Apps
headings: Slack AI, Notion AI and Rovo in the browser
Slack, Notion and Grammarly desktop apps
Grammarly and other AI writing extensions
Keep AI extensions off sensitive sites
body: AI Inside Work Apps Many work apps now have AI built in: Slack AI, Notion AI and Atlassian Rovo in Jira and Confluence, plus AI writing tools such as Grammarly. People use them without opening an AI site, so they're easy to miss. This page explains what Whiteout checks in each, what it can only show, and what you can control. In the browser Desktop app --- --- --- Slack AI Prompts typed into Slack AI are checked The Slack app is shown as AI inside a work app Notion AI Prompts typed into Notion AI are checked The Notion app is shown as AI inside a work app Atlassian Rovo Prompts typed into Rovo Chat on your Jira and Confluence sites are checked — Grammarly and other AI writing extensions Listed, but Whiteout can't see what they send. An optional MDM recipe keeps them off sensitive sites. The Grammarly app is shown as AI inside a work app --- Slack AI, Notion AI and Rovo in the browser The Whiteout browser extension checks prompts typed into the AI composers of Slack (app.slack.com), Notion (notion.so and app.notion.com) and Atlassian sites ( .atlassian.net), the same way it checks a prompt on ChatGPT. A prompt that breaks your policies is blocked or warned about before it's sent. Only the AI composer is checked. Ordinary Slack messages, Notion pages, Jira issues, Confluence pages and comments are never judged, even when they mention AI. The extension acts only when someone sends from inside the app's AI panel. App What's checked --- --- Notion AI The Notion AI side panel and the full-page Notion AI chat Slack AI Slack's AI assistant panel Atlassian Rovo Rovo Chat on your Jira and Confluence Cloud sites These apps change their pages often. If the extension doesn't recognize an AI panel, prompts there go through as normal and aren't checked. Whiteout never blocks a send because it can't read a panel. AI actions with no prompt Some AI features run without anyone typing a prompt: Slack recaps and summaries, Notion's suggested actions such as Summarize this page , and Notion's AI answers in search. There's nothing to check, so these are never blocked . The extension records that the app's AI was used, and it shows as use in AI Footprint. No prompt or page content is collected. Block only the AI Slack AI, Notion AI and Atlassian Rovo are listed under Integrations → AI Applications , organization-wide and per group. Blocking one is a partial block : it turns off only the app's AI panel in the browser. Slack, Notion, Jira and Confluence keep working as normal. The app's card carries an AI only chip. The same applies to the AI built into other work apps Whiteout already covers, such as Copilot in Microsoft 365 and Gemini in Google Workspace: blocking the AI never blocks the app around it. The new site permission To check these composers, browser extension 1.16.0 needs access to the Slack, Notion and Atlassian sites listed above. The same update also adds copilot.com, where Microsoft Copilot on the web now lives (see Web AI sites). Extension force-installed through MDM: the browser grants the access silently when the extension updates. Nobody sees a prompt. Extension installed by the person: when the extension updates to 1.16.0, the browser asks them once to approve the new site access. Until they approve it, the browser can keep the extension turned off or on its previous version, so prompts in that browser may not be checked. Let people know before the update, or force-install the extension through MDM (see Force-install the extension). The extension uses this access only to find the AI composer and its send button. It doesn't read or collect messages, pages or files. In AI Footprint Slack AI, Notion AI and Rovo appear with the category AI inside a work app once someone uses them: a prompt the extension checked, or an AI action it saw. A row that only says someone visited Slack or Notion is never created. --- Slack, Notion and Grammarly desktop apps The Slack, Notion and Grammarly desktop apps are listed in AI Footprint as AI inside a work app , shown as Work app in the table. They never count as Not governed and never raise a finding. They're work apps with AI inside, not AI tools in their own right. Their governance shows as Not applicable (built-in or work app) . For the Grammarly app, the drawer says Whiteout can't see what this app sends. Prompts typed into Slack AI or Notion AI inside the desktop apps aren't checked yet. To have them checked, people can use Slack and Notion in a browser with the Whiteout extension. --- Grammarly and other AI writing extensions AI writing extensions such as Grammarly, Sider, Monica and HARPA AI read what people type, and often the whole page, and send it to their own service. There's no AI composer and no send step that Whiteout could check, so Whiteout can't see what these extensions send. AI Footprint lists them, with the sites they can read, under Third-party AI extensions. You have three options: 1. Allow them , and allowlist them under Manage so they stop raising findings. 2. Block them with your browser's extension policy. See Block AI extensions with your MDM. 3. Keep them off your sensitive sites and let people use them everywhere else, with the setting below. Keep AI extensions off sensitive sites The Browser AI policy setting, under Integrations → Mobile Device Management (MDM) , has a section Keep AI extensions off sensitive sites . In Chrome and Edge, the AI extensions you choose stop running on the sites you list and keep working everywhere else. 1. Under Sensitive sites , list the sites, one per line: a hostname such as intranet.example.com, or a whole domain such as .corp.example.com. Don't include https://, a path or a port. You can list up to 100. 2. By default it applies to every third-party AI extension in Whiteout's catalog. To pick, turn on Only some AI extensions and choose them. 3. Choose Save . From then on, Whiteout adds these entries to every MDM profile and script it generates: Intune, Jamf, Kandji, Mosyle, Workspace ONE and NinjaO

title: Browser Coverage
body: Browser Coverage Prompts typed into AI websites are checked by the Whiteout browser extension, but only in the browser profiles where it is installed and turned on. Someone with two Chrome profiles, a work profile with Whiteout and a personal one without it, can use ChatGPT unchecked in the second. Desktop Guard finds those gaps by scanning every browser profile on the device. On Windows, when AI traffic comes from a browser with an uncovered profile, or from a browser where the extension isn't running at all, AI Footprint raises a finding. --- How the profile scan works Desktop Guard 1.8.51 and later scans the device's browsers every 15 minutes, starting about a minute after it launches. It reads only each browser's own profile files and the browser policy in effect. It never reads browsing history, page content or credential files. Platform Browsers scanned --- --- macOS Chrome, Edge, Brave, Arc, Vivaldi, Opera, Chromium, Aside, Comet, Firefox Windows Chrome, Edge, Brave, Arc, Vivaldi, Opera, Chromium, Comet, Firefox Not scanned: Safari (its extension state can't be read without Full Disk Access; on macOS, Desktop Guard still notices Safari running), Opera's side profiles , and Aside on Windows . For each profile, Desktop Guard reports: Values --- --- Whiteout Installed , Turned off or Missing Installed by Force-installed by IT , Added by the user , Installed by software or Developer mode Last used The day the profile was last used Account Work account , Personal account , Not signed in or Unknown account How the account is decided. Desktop Guard compares the domain of the account signed in to the browser profile with the domain of the person's Whiteout sign-in. A match is a work account; any other domain is personal. Only that verdict leaves the device. The email address never does. If your organization uses several email domains, a profile signed in with another of your domains shows as Personal account , because the comparison is with the person's own sign-in domain. Profiles are identified by their folder name, such as Default or Profile 1 , never by the name the person gave them. Which profiles count. A profile counts if it was used in the last 14 days. Older profiles are listed but never count as a gap. The scan also checks whether your MDM's force-install policy for each browser includes Whiteout. --- Profile without Whiteout The finding is Shadow AI — active , shown as Google Chrome · profile without Whiteout . Its drawer reads, for example: Google Chrome sent traffic to chatgpt.com from a profile without Whiteout. The drawer also lists Profiles without Whiteout , each with its account type and when it was last active. When it's raised. Desktop Guard saw AI traffic from the browser on the device, and the Whiteout extension is running in that browser. But the latest profile scan shows at least one profile of that browser, used in the last 14 days, where Whiteout is missing or turned off. Coverage is judged per browser: a browser counts as covered only when every profile used in the last 14 days has the extension turned on. Why it matters. Network traffic doesn't say which profile sent it, so some of that AI use may have come from the uncovered profile, where prompts aren't checked. The list of uncovered profiles shows where to look. A personal profile on a work laptop is the most common case. How to fix it: 1. Force-install the extension for that browser through your MDM. Every profile gets it, and people can't remove or turn it off. See Force-install the extension below. 2. Or ask the person to turn the extension on in that profile (if it's Turned off ), or to add it. 3. If the profile isn't needed, removing it also clears the gap. The finding resolves by itself once a profile scan shows Whiteout turned on in every profile of that browser used in the last 14 days. Until then, the person also shows as Browser without Whiteout under Coverage → Enrollment . --- Browser without extension The finding is Shadow AI — active , shown as Google Chrome · no Whiteout extension . Its drawer reads, for example: Google Chrome sent traffic to chatgpt.com, and the Whiteout extension isn't running in that browser on this device. When it's raised. Desktop Guard saw AI traffic from the browser, and the Whiteout extension hadn't checked in from that browser on that device around the time of the traffic. Why it matters. Prompts typed into a browser are checked by the Whiteout extension. Without it, nothing sent from that browser is checked. How to fix it: 1. Install the extension in that browser. An MDM force-install covers every profile. 2. If the extension is installed but signed out or turned off, have the person sign in or turn it on. 3. If this use is sanctioned, allowlist the provider (for example openai) under Manage . The extension can't tell Brave, Arc, Vivaldi, Opera and Chromium apart from Chrome. When it runs in any of them, it counts as running in all of them. The profile scan is the precise check for those browsers. --- Where these findings come from Both findings need Desktop Guard to see the browser's AI traffic on the device. Today that means: Windows , with Desktop Guard's network sensor running, a browser that uses the Windows resolver rather than its own DNS, and traffic that doesn't go through a secure web gateway. On macOS , Desktop Guard doesn't observe network traffic yet, so Macs don't raise these findings. Uncovered profiles on a Mac still show under Coverage → Enrollment → Browsers and count as a coverage gap there. When a device's browser traffic isn't fully visible, the finding's drawer says so in one line. See Network visibility for how to fix that. --- Force-install the extension Force-installing through your MDM is the fix for both findings. Each browser reads its own policy, so a Chrome policy doesn't reach Edge, Firefox or Aside. Browser Extension ID Policy --- --- --- Chrome dcbndpnolggjgmclalpdcogigpedlhpn ExtensionInstallForcelist with the entry dcbndpnolggjgmcla

title: Built-In Browser AI
headings: Turn features off with your MDM
Check it on a test device first
body: Built-In Browser AI Most browsers now ship with their own AI assistant: Gemini in Chrome, Copilot in Edge, Leo in Brave, Aria in Opera and the AI chatbot sidebar in Firefox. Some of these can read the page that's open as well as what people type. AI Footprint shows, for every browser on every device, whether its built-in AI is on. A Browser AI policy setting lets you turn each one off, or stop it reading pages, through the MDM profiles Whiteout generates. They appear in Coverage → AI Footprint with the category Built-in browser AI . Desktop Guard reports this as part of its browser profile scan, on macOS and Windows. There's nothing to turn on. --- What's detected, and what's checked Feature Browser Checked before send Browser AI policy choices --- --- --- --- Copilot in Edge (the sidebar, the toolbar Copilot button and the Microsoft 365 Copilot app in an Edge tab) Microsoft Edge Windows: yes, by Desktop Guard 1.8.119 or later. macOS: detection only. Allow, Turn off, Allow but block page reading Gemini in Chrome Google Chrome Not yet: detection only Allow, Turn off Brave Leo Brave No: detection only Allow, Turn off Firefox AI chatbot (the sidebar chatbot) Firefox No: detection only Allow, Turn off Opera Aria Opera No: detection only None. Whiteout knows of no enterprise policy for Aria. Copilot in Edge on Windows. Desktop Guard 1.8.119 and later checks what people type and attach in the Copilot pane before it's sent, the same way it checks the Copilot desktop app. A prompt that breaks your policies is blocked or warned about. If Desktop Guard can't read the pane, the prompt goes through as normal and is recorded as not checked. It also checks the Microsoft 365 Copilot app when Edge opens it in a tab . Some Edge versions show that app as the New Tab page. Browser extensions can't run on Edge's New Tab page, so Desktop Guard covers it, and blocking M365 Copilot Chat under Integrations → AI Applications applies there too. Copilot on copilot.com in an ordinary tab is checked by the browser extension, so nothing is checked twice. Copilot in Edge on macOS is detection only, including the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on Edge's New Tab page. Edge on macOS doesn't expose that content to the accessibility interface Desktop Guard reads, so there's nothing for it to check. Use the Browser AI policy to control it there. Gemini in Chrome is detection only for now. Checks before send are coming. Gemini in Chrome also isn't offered in some regions, or to some accounts. Where it isn't offered, AI Footprint shows Not in this browser . Arc, Vivaldi and Chromium report no built-in AI. AI browsers such as Aside, Comet and Dia have their own rows in AI Footprint. --- What AI Footprint shows There's one row per feature. Open it to see each device and browser it was found on, with: Field What it means --- --- Browser The browser the feature belongs to State Whether the feature is on in that browser. See below. Policy The browser policy Desktop Guard found for it, with its value, for example GeminiSettings = 1 (device-wide). No policy set if there isn't one. Page reading For Gemini in Chrome and Copilot in Edge: Can read the open page , Can't read the open page or Not reported Governance Who checks what's typed into it: Desktop Guard, or Detection and policy only Choose Set browser policy in the drawer to open the Browser AI policy setting. States State Meaning --- --- On The feature is on in this browser Off Someone turned it off in the browser's own settings Turned off by policy A browser policy your IT team set turns it off Not in this browser This browser, or this browser profile, doesn't offer the feature Not reported Desktop Guard couldn't tell whether it's on A browser with several profiles shows On if the feature is on in any of them. Off and Turned off by policy are useful posture: those rows never count as Not governed and never raise a finding. A feature that's On counts under Not governed wherever nothing checks what's typed into it. Copilot in Edge counts as governed on Windows devices where Desktop Guard is running. How Desktop Guard decides "turned off by policy". It uses a policy to set the state only once Whiteout has confirmed what that policy's values mean in the browser. For the other policies, the Policy field shows the name and value exactly as Desktop Guard found them on the device, and the state comes from the browser's own settings, or shows Not reported . Desktop Guard only reads policies that are really enforced on the device by management, so a setting a person can change themselves never reads as a policy. Policies set from a cloud console. A Chrome policy you set from the Google Admin console, rather than through your MDM, reaches Chrome as a cloud policy. Desktop Guard doesn't read cloud policies, so the Policy field doesn't show it. The feature's state still reflects what the browser reports. --- Built-in browser AI in use A built-in AI feature raises a finding only when there's evidence someone used it with nothing checking it, not just because it's switched on. The finding is a Shadow AI — active finding, with the feature and browser underneath, for example Gemini in Chrome · Google Chrome . Evidence of use is either: Desktop Guard saw the feature's panel open on that device, or that browser sent traffic to the feature's own AI service. Whiteout counts this only for services it has confirmed belong to the feature, so it doesn't mistake ordinary use of a website for the built-in panel. Copilot in Edge used on a Windows device where Desktop Guard checks it doesn't raise this finding. Why it matters. Whatever people type into the panel goes to the browser vendor's AI with no Whiteout check. Panels that can read the open page can also send that page's content, including internal apps, email and documents. Severity. High . It becomes critical once it's been seen on 3 or more days. What to do: 1. If the feature isn't approved, turn it off with the Browser AI policy. 2. If people may use

title: AI Apps Connected With Work Accounts
body: AI Apps Connected With Work Accounts People connect AI apps to their work account all the time: a meeting notetaker that joins their calendar, a ChatGPT or Claude connector that reads their Gmail or Drive, an AI writing tool they signed in to with Google or Microsoft. Each one is recorded in your identity provider, whatever device or browser it was done from. Once a day, Whiteout checks Google Workspace, Microsoft 365 and Okta for AI apps people connected with their work account, and shows them in AI Footprint. Finding an app never removes it. Detecting needs read-only access. Removing an app's access needs its own permissions, and it's always an admin action, unless you turn on Remove access automatically . The check is on for every organization that gives Whiteout read access to Google Workspace, Microsoft 365 or Okta. There's no switch to turn it on. See Set up read access. --- What it finds AI apps people signed in to, or gave access to company data, with their work account. Whiteout's catalog includes: Meeting notetakers: Otter.ai, Fireflies.ai, Read.ai, Fathom, tl;dv and Avoma AI assistants and their connectors: ChatGPT (OpenAI), Claude (Anthropic), Perplexity and Mistral AI writing and workspace tools: Grammarly, Notion AI, Jasper and Copy.ai Whiteout recognizes an app by its exact OAuth app ID where it has confirmed that ID belongs to the vendor. Otherwise it recognizes the app by its name. A name match is shown for you to review. Whiteout never removes access for an app it matched only by name until an admin in your organization confirms the app is what it looks like. Only AI apps are reported. Every other app connected in your identity provider is ignored. --- Where it shows Where What you see --- --- Coverage → AI Footprint One row per AI app, with the category Signed in with a work account . Open it to see who connected it, through which identity provider, and what it can reach: Sign-in only (the app sees the person's name and email, not their files or mail) or the work data it was given access to. Integrations → Data Integrations The card AI apps connected through your identity provider : for each provider, whether detecting and removing access are set up, when it last checked, View apps , the Read access settings, and the Remove access automatically switch Findings Unapproved AI app connected , below Use through these apps counts as a work account, because it went through your organization's identity provider. See Personal and work accounts. --- Unapproved AI app connected Unapproved AI app connected means someone gave an AI app access to company data through their work account, for example their mail, files or calendar, and your organization hasn't approved the app. It isn't raised when: the app only signs the person in (their name and email), with no access to data an admin gave consent for the whole organization. That was an admin's decision, not one person's. the app is on your allowlist a connector policy already blocks that data for the app. The Connector still connected finding covers that case instead. See Vendor-Native Connector Control. Why it matters. The app can keep reading that data, for as long as the access stays in place, from any device. Nothing it reads passes through Whiteout. Severity. Medium . It's a decision for you to make, not a policy violation. What to do: 1. Check what it can reach. The finding lists the app, the person, the identity provider and the access it was given. 2. If the app isn't approved, remove its access: choose View apps on the identity provider's row, or remove it in your Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 admin console. Let the person know, so they don't simply reconnect it. 3. If it's approved, allowlist it under Coverage → AI Footprint → Manage → Allowlisted tools , with the catalog key the finding shows. 4. Acknowledge the finding with a note. The finding resolves by itself once a daily check no longer finds the access, or when you allowlist the app. Like other AI Footprint findings, a new one raises the Shadow AI detected notification and goes to your SOC/SIEM destinations. --- Removing access On Google Workspace and Microsoft 365, Whiteout can remove an AI app's access for you, once the remove permissions are in place. One app at a time. Choose View apps on the provider's row, pick the app and the people, and confirm. Whiteout shows what will be removed before it does anything. The dialog is described in Vendor-Native Connector Control. Only exactly identified apps. Whiteout removes access only for apps it identified by their exact OAuth app ID. An app matched by name shows a Confirm option: an admin confirms it's the vendor's app, and removal unlocks for your organization. On Google Workspace, access is per app. Removing an app's access removes all of it at once: Drive, Gmail and Calendar. On Microsoft 365, existing sessions can outlast the removal. Access the app already has can keep working for up to about an hour. You can also choose to sign the people affected out, which signs them out of all Microsoft apps. Okta is detect-only. To remove an AI app there, use Okta's admin console. Remove access automatically The Remove access automatically switch is off by default. When you turn it on (you type enable to confirm), each daily check removes access it finds for AI apps Whiteout can identify by their exact app ID, one person at a time, without asking first. Consent given for the whole organization is never removed automatically. It always waits for you. Every removal is recorded in the admin audit log. People can reconnect an app later if you decide to allow it. It needs the remove permissions on Google Workspace or Microsoft 365. --- Set up read access On the AI apps connected through your identity provider card, the Read access section shows what the daily check reads with, per provider. Keys and tokens you enter are stored encrypted and never shown again. Google Workspace Whiteout reads which AI apps people connected by a

title: Importing Network Logs
headings: Getting logs out of your gateway
How identities are matched to users
body: Importing Network Logs Your DNS and proxy logs see AI use that your endpoints can't show you: people who don't have the browser extension or Desktop Guard, devices Whiteout isn't on, browser traffic that goes through a secure web gateway, and identities that aren't Whiteout users. Importing those logs into AI Footprint turns that AI use into evidence and findings. Only AI-site rows are kept. Every other row is discarded while the file is read. It's never stored. --- Import 1. Go to Coverage → AI Footprint and choose Import network logs . If the Network visibility card lists a gateway (under Show what to do ), its button (for example Import Zscaler logs ) opens the same dialog with the format already chosen. 2. Choose the Log format . 3. Choose Choose file and pick the log. 4. Choose Import . When the import finishes, the dialog shows Rows read , AI rows kept , AI sites , Users matched , Unmatched identities and Findings opened , plus the AI tools it found. Choose View findings to go to the Findings tab. The AI rows appear on the Network activity tab, with the observer Cisco Umbrella DNS log , Zscaler web log or Network log (CSV) . Only admins can import. Read-only viewers can't. Formats Log format What to upload --- --- Cisco Umbrella DNS The DNS log export (.csv.gz from S3, no header row), or an Activity Search CSV export Zscaler web (NSS) A web-log NSS feed saved as CSV or TSV, with or without a header row Generic CSV Any CSV with a header row: a timestamp, a host / domain / URL column, and a user / email or client IP column For Generic CSV , Whiteout recognizes common header names, such as timestamp or time; host, domain, url or dest; user, username, email, identity or upn; and src ip or client ip. If there's a URL column, only its hostname is used. Limits Up to 200 MB per file, as uploaded. Gzip a large log (.csv.gz), or split it into several files. The same file can't be imported twice within 30 days. A byte-identical file is refused, because importing it again would double-count its traffic. The message gives the date it was first imported. One import at a time per organization. Rows the gateway blocked are skipped. A blocked request isn't AI use. A row with a time Whiteout can't read is counted at the time of the import. Times without a time zone are read as UTC. Import recent logs, regularly Findings are based on AI traffic from the last 7 days in your imported logs. Older rows are kept as evidence on the Network activity tab but don't open findings. A finding resolves by itself once that person or identity has no AI traffic in the last 7 days of imported logs, so import new logs regularly, for example daily or weekly, to keep findings current. --- Getting logs out of your gateway These are the exports Whiteout reads. For the exact steps in your console, see your vendor's documentation: Cisco Umbrella documentation and Zscaler Help. Cisco Umbrella. Two exports work: The DNS logs Umbrella writes to an Amazon S3 bucket when log management is set up. These are gzipped CSV files with no header row. Upload them as they are. A CSV export of the Activity Search report. It has a header row. Its timestamps follow your Umbrella account's time zone, and Whiteout reads them as UTC, so expect an offset if your account isn't on UTC. Zscaler. Use a web log NSS feed. You define the feed's output format, and NSS writes no header row. Include at least the time, the user (login), the URL or host, and the client IP. Whiteout recognizes Zscaler's field names when a header row is present, and otherwise works out the columns from the first rows of the file. Save it as CSV or TSV. Other gateways (Netskope, Palo Alto, Cloudflare, Forcepoint and others): export a CSV with a header row and use Generic CSV . --- Privacy The file is read as a stream. Each row whose host isn't an AI site is discarded on the spot. It's never stored, buffered or logged. For AI rows, Whiteout keeps only the hostname, the hour, a count of requests, and the identity. Never paths, query strings, full URLs or byte counts. The uploaded file isn't kept. The audit log records the import: the file name and size, a fingerprint of its contents (to catch a duplicate), and the counts. What counts as an AI site is Whiteout's AI catalog plus any sites your organization has added with Add to catalog . See Web AI sites. --- How identities are matched to users Each AI row's identity (the user, login or email in the log, or else the client IP) is matched to a Whiteout user: The log says Matches --- --- An email address, such as jdoe@example.com The user with that email, ignoring case. Alternate emails from your identity provider match too. A name with an email in it, such as Jane Doe (jdoe@example.com) The user with that email A username, such as jdoe or CORP\jdoe jdoe@<your organization's email domain . If no domain is set for your organization, it matches only when exactly one user has that username. An IP address, or anything else that doesn't match a user No user. These become unmatched identities. All of one person's identities across logs roll up to that person. Rows that name nobody are grouped under one identity, unattributed. What happens next depends on the match: Identity Result --- --- Matched, and the person has a live Whiteout surface on any device Evidence only, on the Network activity tab. No finding. Matched, with no live Whiteout surface on any device AI use with no Whiteout on any device Not matched to any user AI use by someone we can't match to a user --- Ungoverned usage AI use with no Whiteout on any device means your imported logs show a Whiteout user using AI sites in the last 7 days, and none of their devices has a live Whiteout surface: no browser extension, Desktop Guard or IDE extension that has checked in recently. Nothing they sent was checked. Severity: high, and critical once it has been seen on 3 or more days. Common causes: the person was never set up, Whiteout was removed or stopped running on their device, or

title: Network Visibility
headings: How Desktop Guard sees AI traffic
Chrome, Edge, Brave, Chromium and Vivaldi
body: Network Visibility Desktop Guard can watch a device's network for traffic to AI services. That traffic is behind Shadow AI — active findings, including the per-browser findings in Browser coverage. But some browsers look up website addresses themselves, and some networks send browser traffic through a gateway, and in both cases Desktop Guard can't see which AI sites the browser reaches. The Network visibility card in Coverage → AI Footprint shows, per device, whether Desktop Guard can see browser AI traffic, and what to do when it can't. It opens as one line; choose Show what to do (or Details ) to see the counts, gateways and policies below. Whiteout only reports this. It never changes network or browser settings. It doesn't act as a proxy, rewrite DNS, decrypt traffic or capture packets, and it never turns off or works around a secure web gateway. Any change is yours to make, through your MDM. --- How Desktop Guard sees AI traffic On Windows , Desktop Guard's network sensor watches the device's connections and the name lookups made through Windows' own DNS resolver, and matches them against Whiteout's list of AI hosts. It records only the AI host, the process, the hour and a count of connections. It never sees what's sent. That works only when a browser asks Windows to look up the name. Two common browser settings prevent it: Built-in DNS client. Chrome and other Chromium-based browsers can resolve names with their own DNS client, which bypasses the Windows resolver. DNS over HTTPS. Firefox turns DNS over HTTPS on by default in some regions, including the United States, and so can Chromium-based browsers. In both cases the browser's AI traffic is invisible to the sensor. A secure web gateway hides it too, because the browser hands its traffic to the gateway. On macOS , device-level network observation isn't available yet. --- The verdicts Desktop Guard 1.8.106 and later reports how each device's browsers resolve names, whether a proxy or gateway is in use, and whether its network sensor is running. Whiteout turns that into one verdict per device. The card counts devices in each. Verdict Meaning --- --- Visible Desktop Guard sees AI traffic from every browser on the device. Browsers not visible At least one browser resolves names itself, so Desktop Guard can't see its AI traffic. Through a gateway Browser traffic goes through a proxy or secure web gateway. Not observed on this device The device doesn't observe network traffic. Browser coverage comes from the extension and the profile scan. Not reported yet The device's Desktop Guard doesn't report network visibility yet. The same information appears in two more places: Finding drawers. When a Shadow AI — active finding comes from a device that isn't Visible , its drawer adds one line saying the findings for that device may be incomplete, and why. Coverage → Enrollment → Browsers. The Traffic visible column gives the answer per browser: Visible , Not visible — built-in DNS , Not visible — DNS over HTTPS , May not be visible — DNS mode unknown , Through gateway , or — when the device doesn't observe network traffic. --- Visible The device runs Windows, Desktop Guard's network sensor is running, no gateway is in use, and every browser looks up names through Windows. Desktop Guard sees AI traffic from every browser, so the per-browser findings for this device are complete. Nothing to do. --- Browsers not visible At least one browser on the device uses its built-in DNS client or DNS over HTTPS. A browser whose DNS mode Desktop Guard couldn't determine, such as Firefox on its regional default, also counts as not visible. Whiteout never assumes it can see traffic it may not. The card lists each browser that isn't visible, with the number of devices and the policy that fixes it. Copy MDM policy copies the exact settings. These policies put the browser's lookups back on the system resolver. They're the same settings Zscaler and Netskope recommend so their own DNS controls work, so they don't conflict with a gateway. If all browser traffic already goes through your gateway, skip them and import the gateway's logs instead. Turning DNS over HTTPS off in the browser means the browser no longer encrypts its own lookups. They go to the system's DNS like every other app's. Chrome, Edge, Brave, Chromium and Vivaldi Policy Value --- --- BuiltInDnsClientEnabled false (on Windows, a REG DWORD of 0) DnsOverHttpsMode off (on Windows, a REG SZ) Browser macOS preference domain Windows registry key --- --- --- Chrome com.google.Chrome HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Google\Chrome Edge com.microsoft.Edge HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Edge Brave com.brave.Browser HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\BraveSoftware\Brave Chromium org.chromium.Chromium HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Chromium Vivaldi com.vivaldi.Vivaldi Not listed by Whiteout. Check Vivaldi's documentation. macOS configuration profile content (for example, in a Jamf Application & Custom Settings payload or an Intune custom profile for the domain above): Firefox Policy Value --- --- DNSOverHTTPS Enabled = false, Locked = true macOS: preference domain org.mozilla.firefox. Firefox on macOS reads policy only when EnterprisePoliciesEnabled is true, so include it. Windows: registry key HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Mozilla\Firefox\DNSOverHTTPS, with Enabled as a REG DWORD of 0 and Locked as a REG DWORD of 1. Opera, Arc, Comet and Aside These browsers have no enterprise policy for this. Their coverage comes from the Whiteout extension and the profile scan. With Whiteout's MDM deployment payload If you deploy with Zero-Touch MDM, the deployment payload includes these settings for Chrome, Edge and Firefox as a separate, clearly labelled optional block, Network visibility (optional) . Nothing in it is applied unless you choose to: Intune: run intune-fanout.py with --network-visibility (together with --browser-group) to create these profiles. As with the Firefox force-install profile, Mozilla's Firefox ADMX templates must be imported into Intune

title: AI Footprint
headings: What AI Footprint does not see
body: AI Footprint AI Footprint shows the AI on your organization's devices and workloads: what is installed, what is running, what is sending traffic to AI services, and which AI websites and AI browser extensions people use. It includes AI that no Whiteout surface governs. That's how you find shadow AI: AI tools used outside your policies, whether by accident or to get around them. Open it in the admin app under Coverage → AI Footprint . AI Footprint never blocks anything. It finds AI and reports it. Policy checks and blocking stay with Desktop Guard, the browser extension and the IDE extensions. A finding is a prompt for you to look, not an action Whiteout has taken. AI Footprint is on for every organization. There is nothing to turn on. --- What AI Footprint shows What it means Where it comes from --- --- --- Installed AI software on a device: desktop apps, IDE extensions, AI command-line tools, local LLM runtimes such as Ollama or LM Studio, MCP servers in an AI tool's configuration, and third-party AI browser extensions Desktop Guard scans each device every 8 hours and when you choose Rescan . Managed devices also report installed AI apps through your MDM connection. The infrastructure agent reports AI on servers and workloads. Running AI processes running now. They're found by what they do (an AI engine, a model file, an LLM server or AI traffic), not by their name, so renaming a tool doesn't hide it. Desktop Guard's AI process sensor, on macOS and Windows Active Traffic from a device or workload to an AI service Desktop Guard's network sensor on Windows, the infrastructure agent, and DNS or proxy logs you import Web AI AI websites used in a browser The Whiteout browser extension Built-in browser AI AI built into the browser, such as Gemini in Chrome and Copilot in Edge, and whether it's on Desktop Guard's browser profile scan, on macOS and Windows AI inside a work app Slack AI, Notion AI and Atlassian Rovo when they're used, and the Slack, Notion and Grammarly apps The Whiteout browser extension, Desktop Guard and your MDM connection Signed in with a work account AI apps people connected to their work account, such as meeting notetakers and ChatGPT or Claude connectors A daily check of Google Workspace, Microsoft 365 and Okta Vendor audit logs AI use the vendor recorded in Microsoft 365 Copilot and Gemini in Google Workspace The Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace audit logs you connect AI SDK packages and model weight files on disk are scanned only when your organization has that scan turned on. It is off by default. Contact support@groovysec.com to turn it on. Known and uncatalogued Whiteout keeps a catalog of AI tools: apps, extensions, websites, CLIs, runtimes and AI service hosts. A Known chip means the catalog recognizes the tool. An Unknown chip means no catalog entry names it. Whiteout found it from what it looks like or what it does: an AI-style name, an LLM API on a local port, an AI engine or model loaded by a process, or an AI-style website. These are your uncatalogued shadow AI tools , counted in the AI tools found tile at the top of the page. Built-in and Embedded AI is the operating system's own AI, or AI inside a signed app from a known vendor. It is expected, governance doesn't apply to it, and it never raises a finding. Built-in browser AI is different: it's a browser's own AI assistant, and it raises a finding when it's used with nothing checking it. See Built-in browser AI. A single weak signal about an unknown tool stays in the inventory without raising a finding. See Unknown tools. Governed and shadow A tool is governed on a device when a Whiteout surface that covers it is live on that same device. For example, the ChatGPT desktop app is governed where Desktop Guard is running. ChatGPT in a browser is governed where the Whiteout browser extension is running in that browser. Coverage is judged per device: Desktop Guard on someone's laptop doesn't govern the AI on their other computer. A tool with no covering surface live on the device is ungoverned . The Not governed column counts those devices. --- The tabs Tab What's on it --- --- AI tools One row per tool: Tool , Category , Provider , Devices , Not governed , Last active and Last seen . A collapsible Overview above the list shows new AI tools per day and how many installs are governed. Click the device count to see every device and user the tool was found on, with the signals behind it and recent prompt activity where Whiteout records it. Web AI rows also show which kinds of account people used. Processes AI processes the sensor reported, in four views: Needs attention , Named AI , Built-in & embedded and All . Filter by platform, or show Running now only . Open a process to see its signer, path, AI engines, models, auto-start entries and file hashes. Network activity Hourly records of traffic to AI services: Provider , Destination , Observer , Process , Device / source , Hour and Flows . Imported logs appear here too, with the observer Cisco Umbrella DNS log , Zscaler web log or Network log (CSV) . Findings Ungoverned AI that needs a decision. See below. Catalog Tools your organization added to the catalog with Add to catalog . Findings Each finding is one tool (or one person, for imported logs) that needs a decision. Filter the list by status ( Open , Acknowledged , Resolved , All ) and by kind ( All , Installed , Running , Active ). Choose Review to see why it's a finding, the evidence, and a Recommended action . Finding What it means Guide --- --- --- Shadow AI — installed AI software is on a device where no Whiteout surface covers it Shadow AI findings Shadow AI — running An uncatalogued AI process is running on a device Shadow AI findings Suspicious compute An untrusted program uses heavy compute with no proof of AI Shadow AI findings Shadow AI — active AI traffic from a source no Whiteout surface governs, including browsers or browser profiles without the extension Shadow AI findings, Browser coverage AI u

title: Shadow AI Findings
headings: Mute, allowlist, acknowledge or add to catalog
body: Shadow AI Findings A shadow AI finding means AI is installed, running or sending traffic on a device where no Whiteout surface governs it. Anything sent through that AI skips your policies. This page explains each kind of finding, how serious it is, and what to do about it. Findings are on the Findings tab of Coverage → AI Footprint . The Installed , Running and Active filters match the sections below. A finding never blocks anything. Whiteout reports the AI. What happens next is your decision: bring it under Whiteout, sanction it, or remove it. --- How findings work One finding per tool, per device. Seeing the same tool again updates Days and Last seen rather than opening a new finding. Findings that look identical (same type, same person or device, same tool) are shown as one row with a ×N chip, and acknowledging that row resolves all of them. Status. A finding is open until you acknowledge it (you've reviewed it, with a note) or it resolves by itself. It resolves when the tool is no longer found, when a Whiteout surface starts governing it, or when you allowlist it. Alerts. A new finding raises the Shadow AI detected notification in Alerts & Audit → Notifications and is sent to your SOC/SIEM destinations. A finding that flaps open and closed doesn't alert again unless it had been resolved for at least 24 hours. Review. Choose Review on a finding to see a plain-language reason, the evidence, and a Recommended action . Severity Whiteout sets each finding's severity from the facts in it. The first matching row wins. Severity When --- --- Critical AI traffic from an ungoverned source, seen on 3 or more days. A process that claims to be a catalogued AI tool but is signed by someone else. An unknown, untrusted AI process that also starts automatically, runs from a suspicious location, serves an LLM to the network or sends AI traffic. High AI traffic from an ungoverned source, seen on fewer than 3 days. An installed AI tool no catalog names. An AI browser extension that can read every site. An ungoverned local LLM runtime or MCP server. A catalogued tool with Elevated risk. An unknown AI process that is unsigned or untrusted, or that serves an LLM to the network. Suspicious compute from a program that starts automatically. Medium A catalogued tool with standard risk, installed where nothing governs it. An unknown AI process from a trusted, signed developer. Other suspicious compute. Low A catalogued tool marked low risk. --- Installed Shadow AI — installed means AI software is on a device and no Whiteout surface that covers it is live on that device. Category Typical examples What to check --- --- --- Desktop app An AI chat app, an AI meeting assistant Is Desktop Guard enrolled and running on this device? IDE extension An AI coding assistant in VS Code or a JetBrains IDE Is the Whiteout IDE extension installed and active? CLI An AI command-line tool Should this tool be sanctioned and governed? Local LLM runtime Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp server Local models can process any data with no policy check. Enroll the device, or remove the runtime. MCP server A server configured in Claude Desktop, Cursor or Claude Code What does the server connect to? Is the device enrolled? Third-party AI extension Grammarly, Sider, Monica See Third-party AI extensions. Web AI An AI website the extension doesn't govern See Web AI sites. SDK dependency , Model file An AI SDK in a project, model weights on disk Raised only when another signal from the same device backs it up. Why it matters. If no Whiteout surface governs the tool, nothing sent through it is checked. For a tool Whiteout normally governs, such as the ChatGPT desktop app, the drawer says which surface governs it ( Normally governed by Desktop Guard ). The finding then means that surface isn't live on this device: Desktop Guard isn't installed, isn't running, or has protection paused. That's a coverage problem, not an unknown tool. What to do: 1. If Whiteout normally governs the tool, check the device under Coverage → Enrollment or People → Devices , and get Desktop Guard or the IDE extension running there. 2. If its use is sanctioned, allowlist it. 3. If it isn't approved, remove it from the device, or block it with your MDM. 4. If it's unknown and you know what it is, choose Add to catalog to name it. 5. Acknowledge the finding with a note, for example Sanctioned for the data team, tracked in JIRA-1234 . The finding resolves by itself after the next full scan once the tool is gone or governed. --- Running Shadow AI — running means Desktop Guard's AI process sensor found an AI process running on the device that no catalog entry names and no Whiteout surface governs. It was found by what it does (its AI engine, its models, an LLM server or AI traffic), not by its name. Two related findings come from the same sensor: Suspicious compute. An untrusted or out-of-place program has used a lot of CPU or memory for a sustained period but shows no AI engine, model or AI traffic. Disguised local inference and cryptominers both look like this. Impersonation. A process claims to be a catalogued AI tool but is signed by a different developer, or not signed at all. The finding is marked Impersonates and is critical. Why it matters. A running AI process with no Whiteout coverage can handle any data on the device. A process that hides its identity or runs from an odd location deserves a closer look. What to do: 1. Choose View process details and IOCs and review the signer, path, AI engines, models and auto-start entries. 2. If it's sanctioned, allowlist it, or choose Add to catalog and match it by its signed app or signer so it's recognized everywhere. 3. If it isn't approved, remove it from the device. 4. For impersonation, treat the device as potentially compromised: isolate it, collect the binary (its SHA-256 is in the evidence) and investigate. Built-in AI (the operating system's own) and embedded AI (inside a signed vendor app) never raise these findings. To sto

title: Vendor Audit Logs
headings: Seen only in the vendor's audit log
body: Vendor Audit Logs Microsoft, Google and Slack keep their own audit logs of what happens in their business products. When you connect one, Whiteout reads it and shows AI use the vendor recorded, including use that happened where no Whiteout app was running: on a phone, in a desktop app without Desktop Guard, or in a browser without the extension. Connect them under Integrations → Data Integrations → Vendor audit logs . There's one card per vendor, each with its own Connect , so you approve each vendor's request separately. Only metadata is stored. From each record Whiteout keeps who used the AI, which product they used it in (for example Copilot in Word, or Gemini in Gmail) and when. It never stores the prompt or the response text, even when the vendor's log includes them. Vendor log What it shows Needs --- --- --- Microsoft 365 Copilot Who used Copilot in Word, Excel, Outlook, Teams and Copilot Chat, and when Microsoft 365 Copilot licenses, and an admin consent to Whiteout's read-only Discovery app (or the Whiteout app) Google Gemini Who used Gemini in Gmail, Docs, Sheets and the other Workspace apps, and when Google Workspace read access for Whiteout Slack AI apps added to your Slack workspace A Slack Enterprise Grid plan --- What you see Each card shows its status, when it last pulled, and how many items it pulled in the last 24 hours. Status Meaning --- --- Connected Whiteout pulls the log on a schedule: Microsoft 365 Copilot every 3 hours, Google Gemini and Slack every hour Not connected Not set up yet Last pull failed The last pull didn't work. The card shows the reason. Whiteout tries again on the next pull. Not available on this Slack plan Slack's audit log isn't offered on your plan. This isn't an error. AI use from the Microsoft and Google logs appears: in Coverage → AI Footprint , as use of Microsoft 365 Copilot or Gemini in Google Workspace, with the vendor's audit log as its source, for the last 30 days in Activity → AI Activity , with the vendor's audit log as the surface When a Whiteout surface also captured the same interaction, Whiteout matches the two (same person, same tool, within about 10 minutes), so it isn't counted twice. Records are kept for 180 days. Only Whiteout users. A record is matched to a person by email address, including the alternate addresses your identity provider lists. Use by someone who isn't a Whiteout user raises no finding. The Microsoft 365 Copilot log is read only for people who are Whiteout users. --- Seen only in the vendor's audit log This finding means the vendor's own audit log shows someone using its AI, and no Whiteout device saw it. In the Findings list it's an AI use with no Whiteout on any device finding, with Seen only in the Microsoft 365 Copilot audit log (or the Gemini one) underneath. Why it matters. The person used the AI somewhere Whiteout doesn't check: a phone, a desktop app without Desktop Guard, or a browser or browser profile without the extension. Nothing they sent there was checked against your policies. Severity. High . It becomes critical once it's been seen on 3 or more days. What to do: 1. Look at where it happened. The finding names the product, such as Copilot in Teams. 2. Cover the person's devices. Install Desktop Guard and the browser extension on the devices they use, ideally through MDM. See Browser coverage. 3. If the use is sanctioned from a place Whiteout can't cover, allowlist the tool under Manage → Allowlisted tools . 4. Acknowledge the finding with a note. There's one finding per person and vendor. It resolves by itself when there have been no such interactions for 7 days, or when you disconnect that vendor's log. --- Microsoft 365 Copilot Whiteout reads Copilot interaction records from Microsoft Graph, with an app-only consent in your Entra tenant. There's something to read only for people who have Microsoft 365 Copilot licenses. Which Whiteout app it reads with. Where your Whiteout server has the read-only Whiteout Discovery app, the Copilot log uses it. It's the same read-only app that detects AI apps people connected, and it can read, never change. Otherwise the log uses the Whiteout app, the same app as the Microsoft 365 connector. The card says which: Reads with the read-only Whiteout Discovery app , or Reads with the Whiteout app . The permissions Whiteout asks for: Permission Type Why --- --- --- AiEnterpriseInteraction.Read.All Application Read the Copilot interaction records for your tenant User.Read.All Application Find each Whiteout user in your tenant To connect: 1. On the Microsoft 365 Copilot card, choose Connect . 2. If your tenant's existing consent to that app already includes the Copilot permission, the card connects straight away. 3. Otherwise Microsoft's admin consent page opens. Sign in as a tenant admin (Global Administrator or Privileged Role Administrator) and approve. Then refresh the card in Whiteout. Reading with the Whiteout app today? If the read-only Discovery app is set up on your server, the card offers Move to the read-only app . It reconnects the log through the Discovery app, so the Copilot log no longer depends on the Whiteout app's broader consent. Already consented? Microsoft records the permissions in force when you consented. If you consented before the Copilot permission was added, you need to consent again to add Copilot interaction access. Connect takes you through it. If the card says Microsoft 365 isn't set up on this Whiteout server yet , contact Whiteout support. On a self-hosted deployment, your operator sets up the Whiteout Microsoft apps first. See Microsoft's documentation on Microsoft 365 Copilot interaction export for what Microsoft records. Google Gemini Whiteout reads Gemini activity from your Google Workspace Admin audit log, using the same Google Workspace read access as AI apps connected with work accounts. The scope Whiteout asks for: Scope Why --- --- https://www.googleapis.com/auth/admin.reports.audit.readonly Read the Gemini events in your

title: Web AI Sites
body: Web AI Sites AI Footprint lists the AI websites people use in their browsers, with the category Web AI . The rows come from the Whiteout browser extension in two ways: Prompts on sites the extension governs. The extension checks prompts on sites such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini. That use appears as a Web AI row. Visits to AI sites it doesn't govern. The extension (1.14.0 and later) notes visits to other AI sites, such as Character.AI, so you can see AI use that nothing checks. This never blocks or slows a page. The extension records the visit and the page loads as normal. --- Known sites Known sites are in Whiteout's catalog. Sites the extension governs. Prompts typed here are checked against your policies. OpenAI and Anthropic: ChatGPT (web), Claude (web) Google: Gemini (web), Gemini in Google Workspace, Google AI Studio Microsoft: Microsoft Copilot (web), Microsoft 365 Copilot (web) Others: Perplexity (web), Le Chat (Mistral), Grok (web), DeepSeek (web), You.com, Poe, HuggingChat Microsoft Copilot has moved to copilot.com. copilot.microsoft.com now redirects to copilot.com. Browser extension 1.16.0 and later checks prompts on copilot.com and in the Microsoft 365 Copilot app, and blocking Microsoft Copilot under Integrations → AI Applications covers copilot.com too. Older extension versions don't load on copilot.com, so prompts there aren't checked until the extension updates. When Edge shows the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as its New Tab page, the extension can't run there; on Windows, Desktop Guard 1.8.119 and later checks it instead (see Built-in browser AI). A governed site never raises a shadow AI finding. Its row shows how many devices and people use it and, where the extension can tell, which kinds of account they use. If someone uses a governed site from a browser or profile without the extension, that's a browser coverage gap. Sites in the catalog that the extension doesn't govern: Meta AI (web) , Character.AI and NotebookLM , plus any sites your organization adds to the catalog. A visit to one of these raises Shadow AI — installed with the category Web AI , because nothing checks what's sent there. Its severity is medium . What to do: 1. If the site is sanctioned, allowlist it under Manage . Use its catalog key or its evidence key, for example web:character.ai. 2. If it isn't approved, review the person's access. You can block the site with your web gateway or browser policy. 3. Acknowledge the finding with a note. --- Unknown sites An unknown site is an AI site that isn't one of the catalogued tools above. It's either: a domain on Whiteout's wider list of AI services, or a domain that looks like an AI site: it's under .ai, or a part of its name is gpt , llm or chatbot . The row shows the site's hostname, with an Unknown chip and low confidence. Unknown sites stay in the inventory. A visit to an unknown site doesn't raise a finding on its own, because a domain name is a weak signal. Many .ai domains aren't AI chat tools. Promote a site to the catalog when you know it's an AI tool: 1. Open its footprint row and choose Add to catalog . 2. Under how to recognize it, choose This site . It matches the site and its sub-domains, on every device. 3. Choose its governance (usually Recognize only (still flagged as ungoverned) ), its risk, and whether to allowlist it. From then on the site shows as Known . Unless you allowlist it, visits raise findings like other catalogued sites the extension doesn't govern. Your catalog entry is also used to classify imported network logs. --- What the extension collects Step What happens --- --- A page loads The extension takes the page's hostname, for the main page only (not frames inside it). On the device It compares the hostname with the list of AI sites Whiteout sends it (refreshed every 6 hours), then with the rules for unknown sites above. Not an AI site Dropped immediately. It isn't stored or sent. An AI site It adds one to that site's visit count for the day. Every 15 minutes, and when the browser goes idle It sends each AI site's hostname, the day, the number of visits, and whether the visits were in a private window. Never collected: full URLs, paths, page titles, page content, search terms, or any non-AI site. Private windows. If the extension is allowed to run in private windows, visits there are counted and marked private, not dropped. Signed out. The extension keeps counting but sends nothing until someone signs in. How long it's kept. Daily visit counts are kept for 35 days. A Web AI row that nobody has used or visited for 30 days is removed from the footprint. --- The "Read your browsing history" permission To see which AI sites are opened, the extension uses the browser's webNavigation permission. It's required in extension 1.14.0 and later. Browsers describe it in broad terms: Browser What the browser calls it --- --- Chrome, Edge Read your browsing history Firefox Access browser activity during navigation The extension doesn't read or upload your history. It looks at each page's hostname as the page loads, and it discards any site that isn't an AI site on the device, as described above. Who has to approve it: Extension force-installed through MDM: the browser grants the permission silently. Nobody sees a prompt. Extension installed by the person: when the extension updates to 1.14.0, the browser asks them once to approve the new permission. Until they approve it, the browser can keep the extension turned off or on its previous version, so prompts in that browser may not be checked. Let people know before the update, or force-install the extension through MDM (see Force-install the extension). To check who hasn't approved yet, look under Coverage → Enrollment for people whose browser extension stopped checking in. --- What isn't covered AI panels built into the browser, such as the Copilot sidebar in Edge, Gemini in Chrome and Leo in Brave. These aren't websites. AI Footprint lists them separately. See Built-in browser AI. AI featur

title: AI System Register
headings: How the register is used as evidence
body: AI System Register Almost every AI framework starts with an inventory. ISO/IEC 42001 asks you to document the tools and resources AI systems use, NIST AI RMF asks for mechanisms to inventory AI systems (GOVERN 1.6) and to document intended purposes (MAP 1.1), the EU AI Act asks you not to use prohibited practices (Article 5), GDPR asks for records of processing (Article 30), and the Colorado AI Act asks for a public statement on high-risk systems in use. Discovery tells you what AI is in use. Only your organization can say who owns it , what it's for and how risky it is . The AI System Register puts the two side by side: every AI tool Whiteout's discovery has found, with the owner, purpose, risk tier and approval you record for it. Open it from Governance Compliance Evidence AI Register , or with AI Register on the Integrations card. The page is titled AI System Register . Where the tools come from The register fills automatically from AI Footprint discovery. Each row is an AI tool found by at least one of: Desktop Guard , on employee laptops and desktops; the infrastructure agent , on servers, containers and build hosts; an MDM integration , reporting AI apps on managed devices. Discovery finds desktop apps, IDE and browser extensions, local model runtimes, command-line tools, SDK dependencies, model files and MCP server configurations. Installs of the same tool on different devices, or reinstalled later, are grouped into one register row, so your record follows the tool rather than the device. You can't add tools by hand. A register entry can only exist for a tool discovery has actually seen, which keeps the register tied to evidence rather than typed-in rows. If the register is empty, the page says No AI tools discovered yet and offers Open AI Footprint . Deploy one of the discovery surfaces first. The page At the top, six figures summarize the tools currently installed: Figure Meaning -------- --------- AI tools Distinct AI tools currently installed somewhere in your organization Fully recorded Tools with an owner, an intended purpose and a risk tier Unassessed Tools whose risk tier is still Unassessed High risk Tools you've rated High Prohibited, still in use Tools you've rated Prohibited that discovery still finds installed. Act on these first. Approved Tools marked Approved for use The table lists one row per tool: Column What it shows -------- --------------- AI tool The tool's name, with a check mark once it's fully recorded. Underneath: its category, provider, and no longer installed if it has been removed. Users How many people have it installed Owner The business owner's email Purpose The intended purpose (hover to read it all) Risk tier Minimal , Limited , High , Prohibited or Unassessed Approved Yes or No Two switches filter the table: Only incomplete hides tools that are already fully recorded. When every tool is recorded, the page says Every AI tool is fully recorded . Show tools no longer installed ( n ) appears when some registered tools have been uninstalled everywhere. They stay on the register with your record, so you keep the history. Record a tool 1. Click the edit icon at the end of the tool's row. 2. The dialog is titled with the tool's name, and reminds you that an entry is complete once it names an owner, an intended purpose and a risk tier. Fill in: Field Notes ------- ------- Business owner Any user in your organization, or No owner . The person accountable for the tool's use, not necessarily an admin. Intended purpose What the tool is used for, for example Drafting customer support replies . Up to 4,000 characters. Risk tier Unassessed , Minimal , Limited , High or Prohibited . Next review Optional. The date you plan to review this entry again. Approved for use Tick when the tool is approved. Whiteout records who approved it and when, and shows Approved by \<email\ on \<date\ . Unticking it clears the approval. Notes Optional. Up to 4,000 characters, for example the vendor assessment reference or the data classes the tool may process. 3. Click Save . An entry counts as complete once it has a business owner, a non-empty intended purpose and any risk tier other than Unassessed . Approval and the review date don't affect completeness, but they appear in evidence packs. Every save is written to the admin audit log, with the old and new risk tier, approval and owner, and whether a purpose is recorded. Choosing a risk tier The tiers follow the risk-based vocabulary of the EU AI Act. Whiteout doesn't assign them, and doesn't check them against any legal definition. The tier is your organization's assessment: Tier Typical meaning ------ ----------------- Minimal General-purpose productivity use with low risk Limited Use that carries transparency obligations or handles some sensitive data High Use that affects consequential decisions about people or processes regulated data at scale Prohibited Use your organization doesn't allow. Pair it with a block, for example an AI app restriction, so discovery doesn't keep finding it. Unassessed Not yet assessed. This is the default. The register records your decision; it doesn't enforce it. Rating a tool Prohibited doesn't block it. To block an AI app or provider, use Whiteout's policy and app-access settings. Those blocks then appear as AI app and provider restrictions evidence. How the register is used as evidence The register feeds the AI System Register evidence source, which backs: NIST AI RMF MAP 1.1 (intended purposes documented) EU AI Act Article 5 (no prohibited practices) GDPR Article 30 (records of processing) Colorado AI Act 6-1-1703(5) (statement on high-risk systems in use) It reads Present when every inventoried tool is complete, Partial when some are, and Absent when none are. The register also appears in the inventory snapshot each day, so the register's completeness over time is recorded once you track a framework. In every evidence pack: report.pdf has an AI System Register section: the summary figures and a

title: Preparing for an Audit
headings: 5. Review the mappings with your assessor
body: Preparing for an Audit This guide puts Compliance Evidence together into a workflow for an audit or assessment against any of the supported frameworks. It's written for the compliance or GRC lead who owns the audit, working with the security admin who runs Whiteout AI. Each step links to the detailed guide. The single most important point: start tracking a framework before your audit period begins. Daily evidence snapshots, which show policy and coverage state over the period, start on the day you first track a framework and can't be backfilled. At a glance When Step Owner ------ ------ ------- Before the audit period starts 1. Agree scope and start tracking Compliance lead First weeks 2. Close deployment gaps Security admin First weeks 3. Complete the AI System Register Compliance lead with business owners First month 4. Record your own evidence Control owners First month 5. Review the mappings with your assessor Compliance lead Throughout the period 6. Keep evidence flowing Security admin Fieldwork 7. Hand over to the auditor Compliance lead 1. Agree scope and start tracking 1. Agree with your auditor which frameworks are in scope and the exact audit period. 2. In Governance Compliance Evidence , turn on each in-scope framework. Set its Audit period from and to dates, and a Scope note describing what's in scope, for example All employees in the EU entity; excludes contractors . See Track a framework. 3. If your auditor assesses against several frameworks, track them all. The same Whiteout data backs every framework, so there's no extra deployment effort per framework. Audit period dates are whole UTC days, and the end date is inclusive. 2. Close deployment gaps 1. Open each tracked framework and filter to Gaps & partial . 2. Open each control. The drawer's hint says what's missing, for example Deploy Desktop Guard, the infrastructure agent or MDM to build the AI inventory. The Evidence Sources reference lists what makes each source Present . 3. Common fixes that lift controls across many frameworks: Gap Fix ----- ----- Inventory, shadow-AI and register evidence Not deployed Deploy Desktop Guard, the infrastructure agent or an MDM integration for discovery. For fleet rollout, see Zero-Touch MDM Deployment. Identity and access lifecycle Partial Connect your identity provider and let it sync, for example Okta or Microsoft Entra ID. SCIM is covered in Groups, Users and SCIM. SOC/SIEM forwarding Absent Add a SOC destination, for example Splunk HEC or a webhook. Enforced AI-use policy Absent Enable AI-use rules for your groups. If rules are configured and it's still Absent or Partial , your organization was in audit-only mode for all or part of the period, so the rules weren't enforced. Runtime enforcement Absent or Partial with activity logged Audit-only mode was on for all or part of the period; the summary gives the number of audit-only days. This is accurate, not a fault: record the deployment mode in the control's note. AI app and provider restrictions Absent Block the AI apps or providers your policy doesn't allow. Tamper-evident infrastructure log or Model output scanning Not deployed Deploy the infrastructure agent or an SDK (Python, Node.js) for your own AI workloads. 4. Not every gap needs fixing. If a gap reflects a genuine scoping decision, record it (step 4). If it reflects a quiet period, for example no policy changes, explain it in the control's note. 3. Complete the AI System Register Every framework asks first what AI you use. In the AI System Register: 1. Turn on Only incomplete . 2. For every tool, record a Business owner , an Intended purpose and a Risk tier , and tick Approved for use where it's approved. 3. Act on any Prohibited, still in use tools: block them, or record why they remain. 4. Set Next review dates that match your governance cadence. The register's evidence source reads Present only when every inventoried tool is complete. 4. Record your own evidence Filter each framework to Customer-owned , then work through the Supports controls. For each one, open the drawer and fill in Your record : a State : Not started , In progress , Implemented or Not applicable ; an Owner who is accountable for the control; a Note saying where the evidence lives, for example AI acceptable-use policy v3, approved by the CISO 2026-03-02, stored in the policy library , and what's outstanding; for Not applicable , a justification your auditor will read. Records hold text, not files, so point to the documents rather than attaching them. See Record your own evidence. 5. Review the mappings with your assessor Every framework is currently a Draft mapping : it was prepared by the Whiteout product team and hasn't yet been reviewed by an independent compliance specialist. Before fieldwork: 1. Generate a pack for each framework and share it with your assessor. The Control Catalog is a convenient overview. 2. Ask them to flag any control where they disagree with the rating, or where they need more than the evidence shown. 3. Record their view in the control's note. You can't change a rating, but the note prints on the control's page in every pack. 6. Keep evidence flowing 1. Schedule a pack per framework: Monthly , Day of month 1, covering the Last calendar month . 2. Deliver it to your GRC platform through a GRC connection, and by email to the compliance lead with Include a download link in every delivery on. 3. Each month, check: - Generated packs : every scheduled pack completed, and Sent to is green; - the pack's Evidence history : snapshots were recorded on every day, and all still verify; - the AI System Register: new tools are recorded. 4. Download each monthly pack and store it with your audit evidence. Whiteout deletes packs after 90 days. 7. Hand over to the auditor 1. Give the auditor a Read-Only account so they can browse frameworks, controls, evidence and the register themselves, download packs and verify them, without being able to change anything. See Who can do what. 2. Generat
